m5-t1.introduction: A second way to understand “Engagement surveys and response bias”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: A survey item should measure one defined idea
sections.explanation: Engagement, satisfaction and intention to stay are not interchangeable constructs. A practice survey is not a validated psychological instrument.

items.label: Name the construct
items.detail: Choose the specific idea relevant to the decision.

items.label: Write one clear item
items.detail: Avoid leading wording and mixed questions.

items.label: Use a consistent scale
items.detail: Make response options understandable and comparable.

items.label: Pilot the wording
items.detail: Check accessibility and meaning with an appropriate review.

sections.takeaway: Do not draw health, personality or clinical conclusions from a few workplace questions.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Responses and favourable responses have different bases
sections.explanation: The independent synthetic survey scenario has 80 invitations, 48 replies and 30 favourable replies. The same funnel contains two distinct rates.

items.label: Eligible invitations
items.detail: 80 people were invited under the scenario’s rule.

items.label: Replies
items.detail: 48 people responded; nonrespondents may differ systematically.

items.label: Favourable replies
items.detail: 30 of the 48 respondents met the stated favourable definition.

sections.takeaway: Response is 48/80 = 60%; favourable among respondents is 30/48 = 62.5%. Neither establishes the opinions of nonrespondents.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: A mean alone can hide different experiences
sections.explanation: Response distributions and context can reveal disagreement that one average conceals. Sharing still needs a disclosure review.

items.label: Distribution
items.detail: Show the response pattern and counts across the scale.

items.label: Participation
items.detail: Explain who replied and what is unknown about nonresponse.

items.label: Free text
items.detail: Remove identifying details before wider sharing.

items.label: Trust
items.detail: State who can see raw responses and how findings will be used.

sections.takeaway: Describe actual confidentiality controls; never promise anonymity the workflow cannot provide.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

checkpoint.question: Does 62.5% favourable among respondents mean 62.5% of all invited employees were favourable?
checkpoint.answer: No. The denominator is the 48 respondents, not all 80 invitations. The nonrespondents’ opinions are unknown.

m5-t2.introduction: A second way to understand “Retention cohorts and fair investigation”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: Retention needs a fully observed cohort
sections.explanation: A ninety-day measure follows eligible joiners to the same follow-up boundary. Recent joiners have not had the same opportunity to be observed.

items.label: Define entry
items.detail: State the joining event and cohort window.

items.label: Define follow-up
items.detail: Choose the exact day boundary and movement rules.

items.label: Check observation
items.detail: Separate eligible fully observed cases from immature ones.

items.label: Report the result
items.detail: In the independent fixture, 34 of 40 fully observed joiners remain: 85%.

sections.takeaway: Do not count unfinished follow-up as confirmed retention success.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: A group difference suggests questions, not a cause
sections.explanation: Role mix, workload, commute and other unmeasured factors may explain an observed difference. Exit feedback has its own response limits.

items.label: Observed pattern
items.detail: State the rate, counts, cohort and period.

items.label: Plausible explanations
items.detail: List alternatives without selecting a favourite as fact.

items.label: Missing evidence
items.detail: Identify what would distinguish the hypotheses.

items.label: Safe investigation
items.detail: Ask authorised process owners and protect identities.

sections.takeaway: Compare only where sample size and privacy permit, and label explanations as hypotheses.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Improve systems without labelling people
sections.explanation: Retention evidence can support clearer job previews, onboarding or schedule review under appropriate authority.

items.label: Choose a process issue
items.detail: Identify a supported, changeable concern.

items.label: Design a safe pilot
items.detail: Name an owner and the proportionate action.

items.label: Measure intended effects
items.detail: Define the relevant outcome and follow-up.

items.label: Watch unintended harm
items.detail: Keep access, workload and employee trust under review.

sections.takeaway: Do not publish individual “likely leaver” lists or treat an aggregate pattern as a person’s intention.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 3. Act on systems, not speculative labels

checkpoint.question: Should someone who joined ten days ago be counted as a ninety-day retention success?
checkpoint.answer: No. Their follow-up window is incomplete. Keep immature cohorts separate and use the agreed eligible denominator.

m5-t3.introduction: A second way to understand “Learning, onboarding and internal mobility metrics”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: Participation, learning and application differ
sections.explanation: The evidence chain separates attending a programme from demonstrating knowledge and applying it at work.

items.label: Participation
items.detail: Record who had access and took part.

items.label: Learning evidence
items.detail: Use a relevant task or knowledge check.

items.label: Application
items.detail: Observe job-related behaviour using clear, consistent criteria.

items.label: Outcome context
items.detail: Examine operational results without assuming the training caused them.

sections.takeaway: A completed course or high quiz score alone does not prove workplace performance or monetary return.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Before and after need comparable measurement
sections.explanation: Tasks, scales, timing and eligible participants should match. Missing follow-up and other support can distort interpretation.

items.label: Set the baseline
items.detail: Define the task, measure and eligible sample.

items.label: Plan follow-up
items.detail: Use comparable timing and conditions.

items.label: Check missingness
items.detail: Show who did not complete the later measurement.

items.label: Review alternative causes
items.detail: Consider practice, selection and other changes before a causal claim.

sections.takeaway: A before/after improvement is not by itself proof of a training effect.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 2. Use comparable pre and post measures

sections.title: Mobility metrics include opportunity, not only uptake
sections.explanation: A low participation rate may reflect access barriers or missing openings rather than low motivation.

items.label: Eligibility
items.detail: Define who could apply and which roles existed.

items.label: Access
items.detail: Check whether people could discover and use the opportunity.

items.label: Progression
items.detail: Track applications, selection and movement as distinct events.

items.label: Fair review
items.detail: Investigate patterns safely and keep consequential decisions accountable.

sections.takeaway: Use job-related criteria and authorised human review; restrict individual assessment details.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

checkpoint.question: Can a low internal-mobility application rate prove that a group lacks motivation?
checkpoint.answer: No. Eligibility, opportunity availability, communication and access barriers may differ. Investigate the process before attributing intent.
